source_text: Nomen dei patris nemini proditum fuerat. etiam qui de ipso interrogauerat, Moyses, aliud quidem nomen audierat. nobis reuelatum est in filio. iam quis enim filius? nouum patris nomen est. ego ueni, inquit, in nomine patris, et rursus: pater, glorifica nomen tuum, et apertius: nomen tuum manifestaui hominibus. id ergo ut sanctificetur postulamus. non quod deceat homines bene deo optare, quasi sit et alius de quo ei possit optari aut laboret, nisi optemus. plane benedici deum omni loco ac tempore condecet ob debitam semper memoriam beneficiorum eius ab omni homine. sed et hoc benedictionis uice fungitur. ceterum quando non sanctum et sanctificatum est per semetipsum nomen dei, cum ceteros sanctificet ex semetipso? cui illa angelorum circumstantia non cessat dicere: sanctus, sanctus, sanctus. proinde igitur et nos angelorum, si meruerimus, candidati, iam hinc caelestem illam in deum uocem et officium futurae claritatis ediscimus. hoc quantum ad gloriam dei. alioquin quantum ad nostram petitionem, cum dicimus: BANCTIFICETUR \'NOMEN TUUM, id petimus, ut sanctificetur in nobis, qui in illo sumus, simul et in ceteris, quos adhuc gratia dei expectat, ut et huic praecepto pareamus orando pro omnibus, etiam pro inimicis nostris. ideoque suspensa enuntiatione non dicentes, sanctificetur in nobis, in omnibus dicimus.
thought_title: The Father's name revealed in the Son and hallowed in us
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the first petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'Hallowed be your name,' after having explained the address 'Father.'
pass_a_gloss: The name of God the Father had been disclosed to no one. Even he who had asked about him, Moses, had heard a different name. It has been revealed to us in the Son. For now what is the Son? He is the new name of the Father. 'I have come,' he says, 'in the name of the Father,' and again: 'Father, glorify your name,' and more openly: 'I have made your name known to men.' Therefore we ask that it be hallowed. Not because it is fitting for men to wish good for God, as if there were also another from whom good could be wished for him, or as if he would suffer unless we wish it. Clearly it is fitting for God to be blessed in every place and time because of the always due remembrance of his benefits by every man. But this also serves in place of blessing. Otherwise, when is the name of God not holy and hallowed through itself, since it hallows the others from itself? To him that surrounding company of angels does not cease to say: holy, holy, holy. Therefore we also, if we have deserved it, as white-robed candidates of the angels, already from here learn that heavenly voice toward God and the office of future glory. This as far as the glory of God. Otherwise, as far as our petition, when we say: hallowed be your name, we ask this, that it be hallowed in us, who are in him, and at the same time in the others, whom the grace of God still awaits, so that we may also obey this precept by praying for all, even for our enemies. And therefore with the utterance left suspended, not saying, let it be hallowed in us, we say, in all.

choices.english: the name of God the Father
choices.why: Keeps the full phrase as in the source, preserving the emphasis on the Father's name being previously unknown.
Renders the image of those enrolled for future glory, keeping the political/military metaphor of candidacy.
Captures the grammatical point that the petition does not specify 'in us' but leaves the object open.
Uses the traditional English rendering of the petition, matching the liturgical register.
Preserves the legal/functional sense of 'uice fungor' as performing the role of something else.

pass_b_english: The name of God the Father had been disclosed to no one. Even Moses, who had asked about him, heard a different name. To us it has been revealed in the Son. For who indeed is the Son? He is a new name for the Father. "I have come," he says, "in my Father's name" (John 5:43), and again, "Father, glorify your name" (John 12:28), and more plainly, "I have made your name known to men" (John 17:6). So we ask that it be hallowed. Not that it is fitting for human beings to wish God well, as if there were someone else from whom good could be wished for him, or as if he would suffer unless we wished it. Certainly it is fitting for God to be blessed by every person in every place and time, because we always owe him the remembrance of his benefits. But this petition also serves in place of blessing. After all, when is the name of God not holy and hallowed through itself, since it hallows all others from itself? The surrounding company of angels never ceases to say, "Holy, holy, holy" (Isaiah 6:3). Therefore we too, if we have deserved it, are white-robed candidates of the angels, and from this very moment we learn that heavenly voice addressed to God and the office of future glory. So much for the glory of God. As for our own petition, when we say, "Hallowed be your name," we ask that it be hallowed in us, who are in him, and at the same time in others whom the grace of God still awaits, so that we may also obey this command by praying for everyone, even for our enemies. That is why, with the utterance left suspended, we do not say, "Hallowed be it in us," but we say it for all.

problems.quote: For now there is a Son, and that is a new name for the Father.
problems.source_quote: iam quis enim filius? nouum patris nomen est.
problems.why: Source is a rhetorical question: 'For who indeed is the Son?' The English turns it into a statement about the Son existing.
problems.fix: For who indeed is the Son? It is a new name for the Father.
problems.ruling: Latin 'iam quis enim filius?' is a rhetorical question; English renders it as a declarative statement 'there is a Son', altering meaning.

problems.quote: "I have come," he says, "in my Father's name" (John 10:25)
problems.source_quote: ego ueni, inquit, in nomine patris
problems.why: The Latin quote matches John 5:43, not John 10:25.
problems.fix: "I have come," he says, "in my Father's name" (John 5:43)
problems.ruling: Latin 'ego ueni in nomine patris' is John 5:43, not John 10:25; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

edits.old: For now there is a Son, and that is a new name for the Father.
edits.new: For who indeed is the Son? He is a new name for the Father.

edits.old: "I have come," he says, "in my Father's name" (John 10:25)

fixed: Source 'iam quis enim filius? nouum patris nomen est.' is a rhetorical question, so the English statement was corrected to a question.
The Latin quote 'ego ueni in nomine patris' matches John 5:43, not John 10:25, so the citation was corrected.

last_rejected.quote: as if he would suffer unless we wished it
last_rejected.why: Latin "laboret" means "to labor, to work" not "to suffer"
last_rejected.fix: as if he would have to act (or labor) unless we wish it
last_rejected.ruling: laboret can mean 'suffer, be distressed'; 'suffer unless we wished it' fits context of God lacking nothing
